title: CoolDrip
subtitle: An hourglass ice-drip coffee maker paired with a caffeine-tracking app
context: Graduation project at SIVA DeTao School of Design, Shanghai, later entered in design competitions
role: Industrial designer: research, form, structure, CMF, app UI, packaging, appearance model

awards.name: Red Dot Award: Design Concept, winner
London Design Awards, Silver
awards.category: Product Design - Bakeware, Tableware, Drinkware & Cookware

links.label: USC story on the Red Dot win

summary: CoolDrip is an hourglass-shaped ice-drip coffee maker paired with a phone app that estimates how much caffeine remains in the body. When I made it in 2024, my thinking was moving into a new stage. Before this, design for me meant finding a clear need and answering it cleanly, with form strictly following function. Here I began asking what lies past function, and whether the feeling an object gives off is part of what it does.

sections.heading: Past the need itself
sections.body:
The practical starting point came from watching people around me drink coffee as a tool to stay awake through heavy work. Mapping their coffee intake, sleepy moments and sleep quality across the day showed the same loop. The body builds tolerance, sleepiness returns, and the person drinks more. Comparing five brewing methods led to ice drip, which is slow and lets strength shift through drip rate, temperature, time and water-to-coffee ratio.

That functional problem grew out of an earlier upright coffee machine I had built the year before. This time, solving the caffeine problem felt like only part of the work. I was trying to find out what kind of form produces what kind of feeling, and whether that feeling can itself be part of the function, or part of what is worth pursuing.

sections.heading: Waiting built into the shape
sections.body:
Ice drip falls drop by drop, like sand in an hourglass. I kept the hourglass silhouette because watching water fall slowly gives a hint of waiting, making slowness part of the idea.

Sketches narrowed to two stacked cones, a brewing unit on top and a glass carafe below, joined by a collar with a side handle. I cut white foam volumes, compared rows of small cone models in pairs, and tested gripping the upper unit by hand to settle the proportions.

sections.heading: Holding the machinery quietly
sections.body:
Keeping that form meant fitting the mechanics inside the upper cone, including the water tank, inlet controller, fan and heatsink, and cold and hot water modules above a stainless steel powder bowl and glass carafe.

Brewing stays simple. Add ground coffee, fill the tank, and pick Light, Mid, Dark or Hot on the lid. Frosted plastic and PC plastic meet a brushed metal collar, stainless steel, glass and an oak handle.

sections.heading: The app and the model
sections.body:
The companion phone app handles timing across four tabs named Drip, Intake, Stock and Shop. Drip shows live extraction progress with a percentage and a pause button. Intake plots estimated caffeine in the body as a daily curve alongside a red Sleepy button for logging fatigue, while Stock lists coffee kept at home.

I carried the hourglass outline onto a white packaging sleeve over a red inner box and trays, and built a physical appearance model measuring 14 x 14 x 18 cm with a wooden handle and a red pull tab on the lid. Across 2024 and 2025, I received eight international design awards for this work, including the Red Dot Award for Design Concept.
